chunks.chunk_text: Section 2 — Definitions (Chapter I, Preliminary). In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires: ... (9) 'consumer rights' includes the right to be protected against hazardous goods/services, the right to be informed, the right to choice at competitive prices, the right to be heard, the right to seek redressal against unfair or restrictive trade practices, and the right to consumer awareness; (10) 'defect' means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law, contract, or as claimed by the trader, in relation to goods or a product; (11) 'deficiency' means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance required to be maintained in relation to a service, and includes any act of negligence, omission or commission causing loss or injury, and deliberate withholding of relevant information; (34) 'product liability' means the responsibility of a product manufacturer or product seller to compensate for harm caused to a consumer by a defective product or deficient service relating thereto; (35) 'product liability action' means a complaint filed before a District/State/National Commission claiming compensation for such harm; (47) 'unfair trade practice' means a trade practice which adopts unfair or deceptive methods, including false representations of standard/quality/quantity, false warranties, misleading price representations, non-disclosure, and related practices enumerated in sub-clauses (i)-(ix).

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter I > Section 2 (Definitions)

chunks.chunk_text: Section 2(9) — 'consumer rights' includes: (i) the right to be protected against marketing of goods/services hazardous to life and property; (ii) the right to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price to protect against unfair trade practices; (iii) the right to be assured access to a variety of goods/services at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard and to have consumer interests considered at appropriate fora; (v) the right to seek redressal against unfair or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation; (vi) the right to consumer awareness.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter I > Section 2 > Clause (9) 'consumer rights'

chunks.chunk_text: Section 2(10) — 'defect' means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied, or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product, and the expression 'defective' shall be construed accordingly.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter I > Section 2 > Clause (10) 'defect'

chunks.chunk_text: Section 2(11) — 'deficiency' means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force, or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service, and includes: (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer; and (ii) deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter I > Section 2 > Clause (11) 'deficiency'

chunks.chunk_text: Section 2(47) — 'unfair trade practice' means a trade practice which, for promoting the sale, use or supply of goods or services, adopts an unfair method or unfair/deceptive practice, including: false representation of standard/quality/quantity/grade of goods or services; falsely representing second-hand/reconditioned goods as new; false or misleading guarantees not based on adequate testing; misleading price representations; disparaging another's goods/services; publishing bait advertisements; not issuing a bill or cash memo; refusing to take back defective goods or withdraw deficient services and refund within 30 days of the stipulated period; and disclosing a consumer's confidential personal information without lawful basis.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter I > Section 2 > Clause (47) 'unfair trade practice'

chunks.chunk_text: Chapter VI — Product Liability (Sections 82-87). Applies to every claim for compensation under a product liability action for harm caused by a defective product (Sec 82). A product liability action may be brought against a product manufacturer, product service provider, or product seller (Sec 83). A manufacturer is liable if the product has a manufacturing defect, a design defect, deviates from manufacturing specs, fails to conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate usage instructions/warnings (Sec 84) — and is liable even without proof of negligence or fraud. A service provider is liable for faulty/imperfect/deficient/inadequate service, negligence, withheld information, inadequate warnings, or non-conformance to warranty (Sec 85). A seller who is not the manufacturer is liable only in specific circumstances: substantial control over design/manufacture, own alteration causing harm, own independent express warranty, unidentifiable manufacturer, or failure of reasonable care in assembly/inspection (Sec 86). Exceptions: no action lies for misuse/alteration after sale; manufacturer not liable if warnings were properly given to an employer/intermediate purchaser/expert supervisor, or if the consumer was under unprescribed intoxicant influence, or for dangers that are obvious/commonly known (Sec 87).

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter VI (Sections 82-87)

chunks.chunk_text: Section 84(1) — A product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action if: (a) the product contains a manufacturing defect; or (b) the product is defective in design; or (c) there is a deviation from manufacturing specifications; or (d) the product does not conform to the express warranty; or (e) the product fails to contain adequate instructions of correct usage to prevent harm, or a warning regarding improper/incorrect usage. Section 84(2) — the manufacturer is liable even if he proves he was not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter VI > Section 84 (Liability of product manufacturer)

chunks.chunk_text: Section 85 — A product service provider shall be liable in a product liability action if: (a) the service was faulty, imperfect, deficient or inadequate in quality/nature/manner of performance as required by law, contract or otherwise; or (b) there was an act of omission, commission, negligence, or conscious withholding of information that caused harm; or (c) the service provider did not issue adequate instructions or warnings to prevent harm; or (d) the service did not conform to the express warranty or contract terms.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter VI > Section 85 (Liability of product service provider)

chunks.chunk_text: Section 39 — Findings of District Commission. Where satisfied that a complaint is proved, the District Commission may order the opposite party to: remove the defect; replace the goods; refund the price/charges with interest; pay compensation for loss or injury due to negligence (including punitive damages); pay compensation under a Chapter VI product liability action; remove defects/deficiencies; discontinue the unfair/restrictive trade practice; not offer or withdraw hazardous goods; cease manufacture of hazardous goods; pay a sum (minimum 25% of value) where numerous unidentifiable consumers suffered loss; issue a corrective advertisement; provide adequate costs to parties; and cease/desist from misleading advertisement.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter IV > Section 39 (Findings/Reliefs of District Commission)

chunks.chunk_text: Section 69(1) — The District Commission, State Commission or National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. Section 69(2) — a complaint may still be entertained after that period if the complainant satisfies the Commission that there was sufficient cause for the delay, provided the Commission records its reasons for condoning the delay in writing.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter IV > Section 69 (Limitation period)

chunks.chunk_text: [BARE ACT TEXT - PECUNIARY FIGURES SUPERSEDED, KEPT FOR REFERENCE ONLY] Section 34(1): District Commission jurisdiction where consideration does not exceed Rs. 1 crore. Section 47(1)(a)(i): State Commission jurisdiction where consideration exceeds Rs. 1 crore but does not exceed Rs. 10 crore. Section 58(1)(a)(i): National Commission jurisdiction where consideration exceeds Rs. 10 crore. NOTE: these figures were revised by a Central Government notification dated 30 December 2021, which lowered the breakpoints to Rs. 50 lakh (District) and Rs. 2 crore (State/National split) — see the companion 'current' chunk below. Do not let Stage 4 cite this chunk's figures without the amendment.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter IV > Sections 34, 47, 58 (Pecuniary jurisdiction - ORIGINAL 2019 figures)

chunks.chunk_text: Section 35(1) — Manner in which complaint shall be made. A consumer dispute complaint in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided may be filed with a District Commission by: (a) the consumer to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided; (b) any recognised consumer association; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest; or (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Chapter IV > Section 35 (Manner in which complaint shall be made)

chunks.chunk_text: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 (notified under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019). Applies to all goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic networks, including marketplace e-commerce entities and sellers. Defines marketplace e-commerce entity as an information technology platform facilitating transactions between buyers and sellers. Sets mandatory duties for marketplace entities and sellers regarding grievance redressal, return/refund, disclosure of legal seller details, and prohibition of unfair trade practices.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020

chunks.chunk_text: Rule 4 & 5 — Duties and Liabilities of Marketplace E-Commerce Entities. Every marketplace e-commerce entity shall: (1) provide in a clear and accessible manner on its platform details about the legal name, principal address, customer care number, and grievance officer; (2) acknowledge receipt of consumer complaint within forty-eight hours and redress the complaint within one month; (3) display prominently all relevant details of registered sellers including legal identity, address, customer reviews, and contact information; (4) not refuse to take back goods, or withdraw or discontinue services, if such goods or services are defective, deficient, spurious or delivered late; (5) facilitate return and refund where goods/services do not meet represented standards or specifications.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Rules 4 & 5 > Duties of Marketplace E-Commerce Entities

chunks.chunk_text: Rule 6 — Duties of Sellers on Marketplace. No seller on an e-commerce marketplace shall: (1) adopt any unfair trade practice whether in the course of the offer on the platform or otherwise; (2) falsely represent himself as a consumer and post fake reviews or misrepresent quality of goods/services; (3) refuse to take back goods, or discontinue services, or refuse to refund consideration paid, if such goods are defective, deficient, spurious, or if the characteristics or features do not conform to what was represented on the platform; (4) guarantee that the goods/services have clear terms of express warranty and comply with all legal obligations.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Rule 6 > Duties of Sellers on Marketplace

chunks.document_title: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, State Commission and National Commission) Rules, 2021
chunks.chunk_text: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 896(E), notified 30 December 2021 under CPA 2019). Rule 3: District Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees (Rs. 50,00,000). Rule 4: State Commission has jurisdiction where consideration paid exceeds fifty lakh rupees but does not exceed two crore rupees (Rs. 2,00,00,000). Rule 5: National Commission has jurisdiction where consideration paid exceeds two crore rupees. Note: Pecuniary jurisdiction is calculated exclusively on the value of goods or services paid as consideration, not on additional compensation or punitive damages claimed.

metadata.hierarchy_path: Consumer Protection Rules, 2021 > Rules 3, 4, 5 (Pecuniary Jurisdiction)

chunks.document_title: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, State Commission and National Commission) Rules, 2021
chunks.chunk_text: Rule 3 — Pecuniary Jurisdiction of District Commission. The District Commission shall have jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees (Rs. 50,00,000).

metadata.hierarchy_path: Rules 2021 > Rule 3 (District Commission Pecuniary Jurisdiction)

chunks.chunk_text: e-Jagriti National Consumer Disputes Redressal Portal — Official Filing Guide for Consumers. e-Jagriti provides end-to-end digital filing of consumer complaints before District, State, and National Consumer Commissions. The portal requires structured information on Complainant, Opposite Parties, Transaction Particulars, Incident Chronology, Grounds of Complaint, Relies Claimed, and Supporting Document Annexures.

metadata.hierarchy_path: e-Jagriti > General Filing Guidelines

chunks.chunk_text: e-Jagriti Guidance on Complainant and Opposite Party Entities. Every consumer complaint must identify the full name, postal address with PIN code, email, and mobile contact of the Complainant. Opposite Parties must be distinguished by their respective commercial role: (1) Registered Merchant / Seller who issued the bill/invoice; (2) Product Manufacturer or Brand owner liable for manufacturing defects; (3) E-Commerce Platform Intermediary if purchased online; (4) Authorized Service Center if warranty service was refused or deficient. Legal addresses must be provided for service of court summons.

metadata.hierarchy_path: e-Jagriti > Filing Guide > Complainant and Opposite Party Details

chunks.chunk_text: e-Jagriti Guidance on Transaction Details & Consideration Paid. The complaint form requires product or service description, model/serial identification, purchase or invoice date, invoice number, and exact consideration paid in Indian Rupees (INR). Under the Consumer Protection Rules 2021, the consideration actually paid determines the Pecuniary Jurisdiction of the Commission (District up to Rs. 50 Lakhs). Compensation or damage claims do not alter the pecuniary jurisdiction threshold.

metadata.hierarchy_path: e-Jagriti > Filing Guide > Transaction Details and Consideration

chunks.chunk_text: e-Jagriti Evidence and Mandatory Annexure Checklist. The following documents must be uploaded and indexed in the Annexures: (1) Mandatory: Tax invoice, purchase bill, cash memo, or proof of payment showing consideration paid; (2) Mandatory: Written grievance notice, email communications, or customer support ticket history showing the seller/manufacturer was notified of the defect; (3) Where applicable: Manufacturer warranty card, service job sheet, technician inspection report, or service refusal report; (4) Helpful supporting evidence: Photographs or videos of physical defect, chat transcripts, payment gateway statements. Each annexure must be referenced in the statement of facts.

metadata.hierarchy_path: e-Jagriti > Filing Guide > Evidence Checklist & Annexures

chunks.chunk_text: e-Jagriti Guidance on Itemized Reliefs (Prayer under Section 39). The complaint must clearly distinguish: (a) Principal statutory remedy: replacement of defective good or full refund of consideration paid with reasonable interest; (b) Compensation: damages for mental harassment, distress, or inconvenience caused by deficiency in service; (c) Litigation expenses: reasonable legal and filing costs. The complainant should not inflate claims arbitrarily; each head of relief must be stated with clarity.

metadata.hierarchy_path: e-Jagriti > Filing Guide > Relief and Prayer Formulation

chunks.chunk_text: e-Jagriti Territorial Jurisdiction and Limitation Period. Under Section 69 CPA 2019, a complaint must be filed within two (2) years from the date on which the cause of action arose (e.g. date of defect discovery or refusal of warranty). Under Section 34(2), the complaint can be filed in the District Commission where the complainant resides or personally works for gain, or where the cause of action wholly or partially arose, which includes the delivery address in online purchases.

metadata.hierarchy_path: e-Jagriti > Filing Guide > Territorial Jurisdiction & Limitation
